name: Finnic
region: Around the Gulf of Finland: Finland, Estonia, Karelia and the Ingrian and Livonian coasts
defining_innovation: Assibilation: *t became s before i, which is why Finnish has vesi 'water' but the case form veden, from Proto-Uralic *weti.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
Proto-Finnic was spoken around the Gulf of Finland, probably in the late first millennium BCE, and its descendants still form a close-knit group. A Finn and an Estonian can recognise much of each other's vocabulary, though they need practice to understand each other's speech. Finnic is also the most conservative branch in sound structure: Finnish *kala* 'fish' and *nimi* 'name' look almost exactly like their Proto-Uralic reconstructions.

Finnic shows the result of long contact with Indo-European neighbours more clearly than any other branch. Baltic gave words such as *hammas* 'tooth' and *heinä* 'hay'. Germanic gave *kuningas* 'king', *rengas* 'ring' and *kaunis* 'beautiful', in forms older than any attested Germanic language (the Germanic tree cites the same words).

chapters.title: Finnish and Estonian
chapters.body:
Both languages were first written in the Reformation. **Mikael Agricola**, a student of Luther's Wittenberg, published a Finnish primer (*Abckiria*, 1543) and a New Testament (1548), and his spelling, modelled on Swedish, German and Latin, set the course for written Finnish. Estonian printing began at about the same time, but under German-speaking clergy and landowners, which shows in its early spelling and vocabulary.

Estonian changed more than Finnish. It lost many final vowels and developed a three-way contrast of length (short, long, overlong) that distinguishes words such as *linna* 'of the town' and *linna* 'to the town' by quantity alone.

chapters.title: National Languages and Small Ones
chapters.body:
In the 19th century Finnish went from peasant speech to national language. Elias Lönnrot compiled the *Kalevala* (1835, expanded 1849) from oral poetry, and a language decree of 1863 began to put Finnish on an equal footing with Swedish in administration. Estonian became a state language with independence in 1918, and again in 1991.

The small Finnic languages fared worse. Votic has only a handful of elderly speakers. Livonian, once spoken along the coast of Latvia, lost its last native speaker in 2013, although it is still learned and taught as a heritage language.

speakers.note: Finnish (about 5 million) and Estonian (about 1 million) are safe; Karelian, Veps and Votic are endangered, and Livonian has no native speakers.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.
Moseley, Christopher, ed. 2010. Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger, 3rd ed. Paris: UNESCO Publishing.
Statistics Finland. Population structure: population by language.

turning_points.title: Assibilation: *ti → si
turning_points.description: `*t` becomes `s` before `*i`. Finnish *vesi* 'water' comes from `*weti`, while the genitive *veden* keeps the old consonant because no *i* followed it. The alternation survives in many Finnish words.

sources.citation: Kallio, Petri. 2006. Suomen kantakielten absoluuttista kronologiaa. Virittäjä 110.
Abondolo, Daniel, ed. 1998. The Uralic Languages. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Baltic and Germanic loanwords
turning_points.description: Baltic and then Germanic neighbours contribute hundreds of words, including *hammas* 'tooth', *kuningas* 'king' and *rengas* 'ring'. The Germanic loans preserve endings like `*-az` that no Germanic text records, which makes them evidence for Proto-Germanic itself.

sources.citation: Kallio, Petri. 2006. Suomen kantakielten absoluuttista kronologiaa. Virittäjä 110.

turning_points.title: Consonant gradation
turning_points.description: Stops weaken when the syllable closes: Finnish *kukka* 'flower' : *kukan* 'of the flower', *pata* 'pot' : *padan*. Saami has a similar system, and whether it was inherited from a shared ancestor or developed separately through contact is disputed.
turning_points.notation: kk pp tt → k p t · k p t → ∅ v d in closed syllables (kukka : kukan, pata : padan)

sources.citation: Abondolo, Daniel, ed. 1998. The Uralic Languages. London: Routledge.
Sammallahti, Pekka. 1998. The Saami Languages: An Introduction. Kárášjohka: Davvi Girji.

turning_points.title: Agricola's Finnish
turning_points.description: Mikael Agricola's primer (1543) and New Testament (1548) are the first books in Finnish. His Latin-alphabet spelling, drawing on Swedish, German and Latin habits, is the ancestor of modern Finnish orthography.

sources.citation: Bakró-Nagy, Marianne, Johanna Laakso & Elena Skribnik, eds. 2022. The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.title: The Kalevala and the 1863 decree
turning_points.description: Lönnrot's *Kalevala* makes Finnish a language of national literature, and the language decree of 1863 begins to raise it to equal status with Swedish, the language of administration and education.

sources.citation: Bakró-Nagy, Marianne, Johanna Laakso & Elena Skribnik, eds. 2022. The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.title: Livonian's last native speaker
turning_points.description: Grizelda Kristiņa, the last person to speak Livonian as a first language, dies. The language survives in a small community of learners and in Latvian place names along the Livonian coast.

sources.citation: Bakró-Nagy, Marianne, Johanna Laakso & Elena Skribnik, eds. 2022. The Oxford Guide to the Uralic Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
